Why this guide was rebuilt The original version of this guide was drafted before the Pathology of Blood Vessels and Atherosclerosis ELS sessions corrected several points. This version is rebuilt from the actual Student Study Guides (with key) and the ELS session slides, and folds in the corrections made live in session: elevated LDL (not HDL) drives atherosclerosis risk, Central Asia (not the U.S.) currently has the highest atherosclerosis prevalence, and vinyl chloride itself (not polyvinyl chloride) is the angiosarcoma carcinogen — PVC manufacturing exposes workers to vinyl chloride, but the polymer is not the carcinogen. All histology/gross/angiography images below are pulled directly from the course materials.

1. Arteriosclerosis Family & Atherosclerosis

SDL: Pathology of Blood Vessels I · Atherosclerosis ELS

1.1 What is arteriosclerosis, broadly?

Arteriosclerosis is thickening of the arterial wall resulting in loss of elasticity and/or occlusion of blood flow. It is an umbrella term for three distinct processes:

ProcessVessel Layer / ChangeHistologic Look
ArteriolosclerosisThickening of small arteries/arteriolesHyaline (homogeneous pink ring) or hyperplastic (“onion-skin” laminated rings)
Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosisCalcification of the mediaDark purple/basophilic calcified clusters within the medial wall; does not narrow the lumen and is usually clinically silent
AtherosclerosisThickening of the intima from lipid plaque (atheroma) formationFibrofatty plaque with a lipid/necrotic core beneath a fibrous cap

1.2 Risk factors

ModifiableNon-modifiable
Hyperlipidemia/hypercholesterolemia, hypertension, smoking, systemic inflammation, chronic stress, sedentary lifestyle, obesity, diabetesGenetic predisposition, family history, older age, male sex
Corrected in session Not every risk factor is modifiable — the ELS explicitly flagged this as a common trap answer (“all risk factors are modifiable” is false). Age, sex, and genetics/family history cannot be changed.

1.3 The endothelial response-to-injury hypothesis

Atherosclerosis is best understood as a chronic inflammatory and healing response to repeated endothelial injury. The healing process itself — meant to repair the vessel — is what builds the plaque and drives downstream disease.

Major causes of endothelial injury:

  • Hemodynamic disturbance — turbulent/non-laminar blood flow, hypertension (branch points and curves are classic sites)
  • Hypercholesterolemia — high LDL, low HDL
  • Inflammation
  • Infection
  • Toxins — smoking

Each of these increases endothelial permeability and leukocyte/platelet adhesion, and impairs endothelial function via lipid accumulation and oxidative stress. Non-laminar flow is the classic initiator; an intimal tear is a much larger mechanical injury that instead produces a dissection, not a routine atheroma.

1.4 Steps of atheroma (plaque) formation

  1. Endothelial injury & dysfunction → increased permeability
  2. LDL accumulates in the vessel wall and is oxidized/modified by reactive oxygen species from inflammatory cells
  3. Platelets and monocytes adhere to the injured endothelium
  4. Monocytes migrate into the intima, differentiate into macrophages, and take up oxidized LDL via scavenger receptors (distinct from the native LDL receptor) → become lipid-laden foam cells
  5. Smooth muscle cells (SMCs) are recruited from the media into the intima (signaled by activated macrophages/platelets)
  6. SMCs proliferate and deposit extracellular matrix (collagen) → forms the fibrous cap
  7. Lymphocytes are recruited
  8. Further lipid accumulation, both extracellularly and within SMCs/macrophages
  9. Calcification of ECM and necrotic debris (late-stage feature)
Not strictly linear Several of these steps happen simultaneously rather than in one fixed order — know the general sequence and what is more typical of an older vs. newer plaque (calcification and a dense necrotic core = older).

1.5 From normal artery to complicated plaque (histology)

1.6 Foam cells & the protective role of HDL

In hyperlipidemia, lipids accumulate within the permeable intima and are oxidized by reactive oxygen species from inflammatory cells. Scavenger receptors on macrophages (and SMCs) recognize and internalize this modified LDL — but the modified LDL cannot be fully degraded, so it accumulates within the cell, forming a foam cell.

HDL is protective chiefly through reverse cholesterol transport: it removes cholesterol from peripheral tissues (including foam cells within plaques) and delivers it back to the liver for excretion. Low HDL removes this protective effect rather than actively causing injury.

Corrected in session It is elevated LDL, not elevated HDL, that increases atherosclerosis risk — higher HDL is protective. Watch for this exact trap on exam-style questions.

1.7 The fibrous cap

Growth factors from platelets, macrophages, and endothelial cells recruit SMCs into the intima and stimulate them to synthesize the collagen that stabilizes the plaque as a fibrous cap:

  • PDGF (platelet-derived growth factor) — stimulates SMC proliferation and migration into the intima
  • TGF-β — key driver of SMC extracellular matrix (collagen) production
Vignette A 60-year-old woman undergoes carotid endarterectomy for severe atherosclerotic stenosis. Histology shows a fibrous cap composed primarily of collagen overlying a lipid-rich necrotic core. Which cell produces this collagen?

Answer: smooth muscle cells — not endothelial cells, macrophages, or platelets, which instead signal to recruit and activate the SMCs.

1.8 Critical stenosis & stable vs. unstable plaque

Critical stenosis is severe luminal occlusion sufficient to cause tissue ischemia, generally associated with roughly 70–75% reduction in luminal cross-sectional area.

Stable plaqueVulnerable/unstable plaque
Fibrous capThickThin
Lipid/necrotic coreSmallerLarge
Immune infiltrateReducedExtensive
Typical disease patternChronic: critical stenosis, chronic ischemia, stable angina, peripheral arterial diseaseAcute: plaque rupture/fissuring/erosion → thrombosis → MI, stroke, sudden cardiac death
Case — how ischemia differs by plaque type Stable plaque: gradual ~70% luminal occlusion → increased resistance → chronically reduced flow past the lesion → ischemia especially with exertion (demand ischemia), though acute change is still possible.

Vulnerable plaque: rupture/fissuring exposes thrombogenic core material → acute thrombosis → sudden complete/near-complete occlusion → infarction. Hemorrhage into the plaque can also acutely expand it.

1.9 Macrophages: from stable to vulnerable

Macrophages actively convert a relatively stable plaque into a vulnerable one:

  • Phagocytose lipid → become foam cells
  • Release cytokines that recruit more immune cells → sustains chronic inflammation
  • Secrete matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) that degrade the collagen of the fibrous cap
  • Undergo apoptosis → adds to necrotic debris in the lipid core

Chronic inflammation + fibrous cap degradation + dense necrotic core = vulnerable plaque

1.10 Imaging correlate: CT angiography & calcification

CT angiography visualizes vessel narrowing from intimal thickening using IV contrast. Calcified plaque appears bright because calcium absorbs x-rays more than soft tissue (same reason bone is bright on x-ray/CT). Calcification is generally a feature of later-stage plaque, though a non-calcified plaque can still be stable depending on other features (fibrous cap thickness, inflammation).

Case — exertional angina, fixed stenosis Identical twins with familial hypercholesterolemia both develop substernal chest discomfort on exertion that resolves with rest; CT angiography shows coronary plaques, one heavily calcified. Severe fixed stenosis lets resting flow meet the heart's lower resting oxygen demand, but flow cannot increase enough to meet demand during exertion → transient ischemia → chest pain that resolves once demand falls with rest.

1.11 Epidemiology

Corrected in session Central Asia, not the United States, currently has the highest reported prevalence of atherosclerosis, related to increasing adoption of a Western diet alongside limited access to cardiovascular healthcare, especially in rural areas. Plaque buildup itself begins early in life, well before clinical manifestations appear.
Practice Questions — Section 1

1. A 52-year-old male has hypertension, smokes, and has an elevated LDL with a low HDL. Which mechanism explains the protective effect of a normal HDL level against atherosclerosis?

HDL's protective effect comes from reverse cholesterol transport — removing cholesterol from peripheral tissue (including plaques) and delivering it to the liver for excretion. The other options describe pro-atherogenic, not protective, processes.

2. Which vessel change is defined by calcification confined to the media, typically without narrowing the vessel lumen?

Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosis calcifies the media (appears as dark purple/basophilic clusters on H&E) and is usually clinically silent since the intima/lumen is not primarily affected — unlike atherosclerosis, which thickens the intima.

3. A 45-year-old male with markedly elevated LDL develops an early atherosclerotic lesion. Macrophages in the intima are laden with lipid droplets. What process most directly produces these cells?

Oxidized/modified LDL is recognized by scavenger receptors (distinct from the native LDL receptor) on macrophages. Because this modified LDL cannot be fully degraded, it accumulates intracellularly, producing a foam cell.

2. Hypertension

SDL: Pathology of Blood Vessels I

2.1 Blood pressure regulation

Blood pressure = Cardiac Output (CO) × Peripheral Vascular Resistance (PVR).

ComponentInfluencing Factors
Cardiac outputBlood volume (sodium handling, ANP/BNP), stroke volume, heart rate, contractility
Peripheral vascular resistanceVasoconstriction (catecholamines, angiotensin II, α-adrenergic signaling) vs. vasodilation (nitric oxide, prostaglandins, β-adrenergic signaling)

2.2 The Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS)

StepMetaboliteProduced In
1AngiotensinogenLiver
2ReninKidney (juxtaglomerular cells) — released in response to low renal perfusion, low blood volume, or sympathetic stimulation
3Angiotensin IBloodstream (angiotensinogen + renin)
4Angiotensin IILungs, mainly (via ACE on capillary endothelium; can also occur in other organs)
5AldosteroneAdrenal cortex, stimulated by angiotensin II

Net effect: angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor and stimulates aldosterone release; aldosterone promotes renal Na+/water resorption → increased blood volume → increased blood pressure. Falling blood pressure/volume is also sensed by cardiac volume receptors, which (via ANP/BNP) promote natriuresis and vasodilation to counteract it.

2.3 Primary vs. secondary hypertension

Primary (essential) hypertension has no single identifiable cause and accounts for the large majority of cases. Risk factors: genetic predisposition, obesity, high-salt diet, smoking, stress, diabetes, alcohol.

Secondary hypertension has an identifiable underlying cause — remember with RENAL:

LetterSystemExample / Mechanism
RRenal dysfunctionRenal artery stenosis (e.g., from fibromuscular dysplasia) → impaired renal perfusion, impaired renin handling, impaired Na+/water excretion
EEndocrine dysfunctionHyperaldosteronism, hyperthyroidism → direct effects on RAAS/vasculature
NNeurologic dysfunctionRaised intracranial pressure → altered neural control of heart rate/vascular tone
AAortic deformationCoarctation of the aorta → impaired renal perfusion (upstream hypertension)
LLabile/transient factorsAcute stress/drugs activate the sympathetic nervous system → ↑HR, ↑vascular tone

2.4 Benign vs. malignant hypertension

Benign (chronic) HTNMalignant HTN
Blood pressureElevated, but sub-emergency>180/120 mmHg, often with acute end-organ damage
Time courseSlow, insidiousRapid, can be life-threatening
Associated arteriolar changeHyaline arteriolosclerosisHyperplastic (“onion-skin”) arteriolosclerosis

The relationship runs both directions: hypertension causes arteriolosclerosis, and the resulting arteriolar narrowing/renal ischemia can further activate RAAS, worsening hypertension — a self-perpetuating feedback loop.

2.5 Complications of chronic hypertension

Ischemic heart disease, cardiomyopathy, heart failure, renal failure, retinopathy, stroke. Longstanding hypertension is also the single most important acquired risk factor for aortic aneurysm and aortic dissection (Section 3), by degenerating the aortic media and increasing wall stress.

Vignette — acute vs. chronic hypertension A healthy medical student is called up in front of the class for a BP demo and measures 150/90.

Most likely cause of this acute reading: an acute sympathetic ("white coat") response → ↑ heart rate → ↑ cardiac output. (Renin can rise too, but its effect on BP is slower/indirect via RAAS; the direct effect of ↑HR on cardiac output is the stronger, faster answer.) This component maps to cardiac output, not peripheral vascular resistance.

If this pattern instead persisted for decades, it is associated with hyaline arteriolosclerosis, atherosclerosis, aortic aneurysm, and aortic dissection — chronic pressure-induced endothelial injury and medial degeneration underlie all four.
Practice Questions — Section 2

1. A young woman is found to have renal artery stenosis with a “string-of-beads” appearance on angiography, and new-onset hypertension. Which letter of the RENAL mnemonic best classifies this cause of secondary hypertension?

Fibromuscular dysplasia causing renal artery stenosis falls under the “R” (renal dysfunction) category of secondary hypertension causes.

2. Which arteriolar histology is characteristic of malignant hypertension?

Malignant hypertension (BP >180/120) produces concentric, laminated smooth-muscle-cell hyperplasia — the “onion-skin” pattern. Chronic/benign hypertension instead produces hyaline arteriolosclerosis.

3. Angiotensin I is converted to angiotensin II primarily within the capillary endothelium of which organ?

Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) is concentrated on pulmonary capillary endothelium, so most conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II occurs there (though it can occur to a lesser extent in other vascular beds).

Section 2 Summary Table

ConceptKey Facts
BP = CO × PVRCO: volume, HR, contractility. PVR: vasoconstriction vs. vasodilation balance
RAAS orderAngiotensinogen (liver) → renin (kidney) → angiotensin I → angiotensin II (lung, via ACE) → aldosterone (adrenal)
Primary HTNNo single cause; genetics, obesity, salt intake, smoking, stress, diabetes, alcohol
Secondary HTN (RENAL)Renal (artery stenosis), Endocrine (hyperaldosteronism), Neurologic (↑ICP), Aortic (coarctation), Labile (stress/drugs)

3. Aneurysms, Dissection & AV Fistula

SDL: Pathology of Blood Vessels I · Blood Vessels ELS

3.1 Types of aneurysm

TypeDescriptionTypical Causes
True — saccularFocal outpouching of the vessel wallAtherosclerosis, infection, congenital defect
True — fusiformCircumferential dilation of the vessel wallAtherosclerosis, hypertension
False (pseudoaneurysm)Tear in the arterial wall with dilation contained by extravascular connective tissue (not a true vessel wall layer)Trauma, surgical access site
DissectionTear in the intima allowing blood to track and bleed within the mediaAtherosclerosis, hypertension, connective tissue disorders, pregnancy

All aneurysms ultimately form from medial degeneration — whatever weakens the structural integrity of the media (atherosclerosis, hypertension, genetic connective tissue defects) reduces the wall's ability to withstand arterial pressure, leading to dilation.

3.2 Site-specific risk factors

SiteDominant Risk FactorOthers
Ascending aortaHypertensionConnective tissue disorders
Thoracic aortaHypertensionConnective tissue disorders, congenital defects
Abdominal aortaAtherosclerosisOlder age, male sex, smoking
Pearl Atherosclerosis dominates for the abdominal aorta; hypertension (and connective tissue disease) dominates for the ascending/thoracic aorta — this contrast is the single most testable fact in this section.

3.3 Complications of aneurysm

ComplicationMechanism
HemorrhageProgressive wall dilation → progressive weakening → rupture → massive internal bleeding
Pulmonary embolismA mural thrombus forms at the site of turbulent/disrupted flow within the aneurysm → shear forces dislodge it → travels to the lungs
SepsisInfection of the plaque/thrombus/wall (a mycotic aneurysm) seeds the bloodstream

3.4 Arteriovenous (AV) fistula

An AV fistula is an abnormal direct connection between an artery and a vein, rerouting high-pressure arterial blood into the low-pressure venous system. The resulting increased pressure/flow through the venous side can dilate the vessel and produce an aneurysm.

3.5 Aortic dissection

Driven by cystic medial degeneration (cystic medial necrosis): loss of structural extracellular matrix within the vascular media weakens the wall, permitting an intimal tear that lets blood dissect into and along the media. Connective tissue disorders predispose by directly causing this ECM deficiency.

Aortic dissections are classified by the DeBakey (and Stanford) systems based on which segments of the aorta are involved — know that this classification exists and is used to guide management (surgical vs. medical).

Case — Marfan syndrome A 24-year-old male, 198 cm tall with long extremities and hypermobile joints, develops sudden severe chest pain radiating to the back. CT angiography shows dilation of the ascending aorta with an intimal tear.

What predisposed him? Young age + body habitus + hypermobility point to a genetic cause of medial degeneration rather than atherosclerosis or longstanding hypertension.

Genetic testing confirms a fibrillin-1 mutation (Marfan syndrome). Fibrillin-1 is an ECM glycoprotein that scaffolds elastic fibers in connective tissue and sequesters TGF-β to regulate its signaling. A defective fibrillin-1 → (1) directly weakens the structural integrity of the vascular media, and (2) fails to sequester TGF-β, so increased TGF-β signaling further impairs medial integrity. Both mechanisms converge on a weakened media that cannot withstand arterial pressure → dilation → dissection.
Genetic vs. atherosclerotic aneurysm — contrast the mechanism Genetic (e.g., Marfan): defect in structural medial components → reduced wall integrity → wall cannot withstand pressure → dilation.
Atherosclerotic (three converging mechanisms): (1) SMCs migrate from media → intima to build the plaque, causing medial thinning/collapse; (2) chronic immune infiltration degrades ECM in the wall; (3) the thickened intimal plaque impairs diffusion of oxygen/nutrients to the inner media → medial ischemia and cell death. All three weaken the wall independently of any single genetic defect.
Practice Questions — Section 3

1. A patient develops a pulsatile hematoma at a femoral arterial catheterization site, with the dilation contained only by surrounding connective tissue rather than a vessel wall. This best describes a:

A false aneurysm results from a wall tear with the resulting dilation contained by extravascular connective tissue, not a true arterial wall layer — classically from trauma or a vascular access site.

2. Which aortic aneurysm site is most strongly associated with atherosclerosis rather than hypertension as the dominant risk factor?

Abdominal aortic aneurysms are most strongly linked to atherosclerosis (plus age, male sex, smoking), while ascending/thoracic aneurysms are more strongly linked to hypertension and connective tissue disorders.

3. In Marfan syndrome, increased TGF-β signaling contributes to aortic wall weakening primarily because fibrillin-1 normally:

Fibrillin-1 normally binds and sequesters TGF-β within the ECM, limiting how much is available to signal. A defective fibrillin-1 releases this restraint, so TGF-β signaling increases and further impairs medial integrity — on top of the direct scaffolding loss from the fibrillin-1 defect itself.

4. Venous & Lymphatic Disease

SDL: Pathology of Blood Vessels I · Blood Vessels ELS

4.1 Varicosities

TypeDefinitionCause(s)
Lower extremity varicose veinsTortuous, abnormally dilated superficial veinsProlonged standing, pregnancy, obesity; female sex & family history increase risk
Esophageal varicesEnlarged veins at the gastroesophageal junctionPortal hypertension from liver cirrhosis
HemorrhoidsEnlarged veins of the rectum/anusStraining (labor, bowel movements, heavy lifting)
Vignette — chronic venous insufficiency A 61-year-old woman with longstanding varicose veins develops chronic, bilateral aching and swelling of the lower legs, worse after prolonged standing, with no acute tenderness, erythema, or unilateral calf swelling.

Diagnosis: chronic venous insufficiency — valvular incompetence lets blood pool, and the resulting venous hypertension produces chronic, bilateral, dependent swelling. This is distinguished from:
  • DVT — typically acute, unilateral, tender, warm/erythematous
  • Migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome) — recurrent thrombosis in different superficial veins, associated with occult malignancy; painful/inflamed veins rather than dependent edema
  • Lymphatic filariasis — parasitic lymphatic obstruction causing severe lymphedema (elephantiasis); nothing here suggests parasitic exposure

4.2 Virchow's Triad & venous thrombosis

ComponentContribution to Thrombus
Endothelial injuryExposes procoagulant subendothelial material, initiating thrombus formation
HypercoagulabilityDrives excessive clotting at the site of injury, allowing progressive thrombus buildup
Stasis of blood flowLeaves a growing thrombus undisturbed and prevents dilution of activated clotting factors

Virchow's Triad is classically taught for venous thrombosis, though its components can also contribute to arterial thrombosis.

4.3 Arterial vs. venous thrombosis

Arterial ThrombusVenous Thrombus
CauseRupture of a vulnerable atherosclerotic plaque; turbulent flowVirchow's Triad — endothelial injury, hypercoagulability, stasis
CompositionPlatelet-richRBC- and fibrin-rich
Major complicationInfarction (MI, stroke) from partial/complete arterial occlusionDeep vein thrombosis → pulmonary embolism

4.4 Thrombophlebitis / DVT

Risk factors: prolonged immobilization, surgery, cancer, pregnancy, genetic predisposition (thrombophilias), obesity.

Major complications: pulmonary embolism (most important), post-thrombotic syndrome, chronic venous insufficiency, inferior vena cava syndrome.

4.5 Lymphatic disease

EntityDefinitionCause
LymphangitisInflammation of lymphatic vesselsMost often infection
Primary lymphedemaLymphedema from congenital/developmental lymphatic defectsCongenital malformation, Milroy disease; lymphatics were abnormal from the start
Secondary lymphedemaLymphedema from obstruction of previously normal lymphaticsTumor/nodal metastasis, lymph node removal (surgery), post-radiation fibrosis, filariasis
Vignette — secondary lymphedema A 52-year-old woman with breast cancer develops a new lymph node metastasis obstructing nearby lymphatics.

Most likely: secondary lymphedema — her lymphatics were presumably normal before being mechanically obstructed by tumor. Not primary lymphedema (that implies a pre-existing congenital defect), not lymphangitis (no infection/inflammation described), and not a lymphangioma (a benign developmental lesion, not something metastatic obstruction produces).

Clinical sign: peau d'orange — orange-peel-like skin dimpling seen with lymphedema/lymphatic obstruction.
Practice Questions — Section 4

1. Which feature best distinguishes a venous thrombus from an arterial thrombus?

Arterial thrombi form on ruptured plaques in fast-flowing, turbulent blood and are platelet-rich. Venous thrombi form in stasis-prone, low-flow beds via Virchow's Triad and are rich in RBCs and fibrin.

2. A patient with a known malignancy develops recurrent, painful thrombosis in different superficial veins over several months. This pattern is classically known as:

Migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome) is recurrent thrombosis in different superficial veins, classically a paraneoplastic phenomenon associated with occult malignancy (particularly pancreatic adenocarcinoma).

3. Which of Virchow's Triad components is most directly responsible for initiating a thrombus by exposing procoagulant material?

Endothelial injury exposes subendothelial procoagulant material, initiating thrombus formation; hypercoagulability then accelerates its growth, and stasis leaves it undisturbed and prevents dilution of clotting factors.

5. Vasculitis

SDL: Pathology of Blood Vessels II · Blood Vessels ELS

5.1 Infectious vs. immune-mediated vasculitis

TypeMechanism
Infectious vasculitisDirect infection of the vessel by a pathogen; damage from the organism itself plus the ensuing immune response
Immune-mediated vasculitisInflammation from an abnormal immune response within the vessel wall (autoimmune); no direct pathogen present in the vessel

5.2 Organizing the vasculitides

Vessel SizeEntities
LargeGiant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis
MediumPolyarteritis nodosa (PAN), Buerger's disease (thromboangiitis obliterans), Kawasaki disease
SmallMicroscopic polyangiitis (MPA), granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA, “Wegener's”), eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA, “Churg-Strauss”), IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura), cryoglobulinemic vasculitis
ANCA StatusEntities
PR3-ANCAGPA
MPO-ANCAMPA, EGPA
No ANCA dependenceAll others (giant cell arteritis, Takayasu, PAN, Buerger's, Kawasaki, IgA vasculitis, cryoglobulinemia)
GranulomasEntities
PresentGiant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis, GPA, EGPA
AbsentAll others — note Buerger's disease shows microabscesses, which are not considered granulomatous
Pauci-immune “Pauci-immune” describes ANCA-associated vasculitis: there is clear immune activity/damage occurring in the vessel wall, but no antibody deposition or immune complexes are found on histology.

5.3 Two mechanisms of vessel injury

MechanismSequence
ANCA-associatedAutoantibodies form against neutrophil cytoplasmic antigens (PR3 or MPO, transiently expressed on the neutrophil surface upon priming) → ANCA binds and activates neutrophils → activated neutrophils adhere to endothelium → damage via reactive oxygen species and proteolytic enzymes
Immune complex-mediatedCirculating antibody-antigen complexes form in response to a stimulus (infection, drugs) → complexes deposit in small vessel walls → activate complement → recruits neutrophils → local inflammatory damage
Case — contrast the two mechanisms Patient 1: a 13-year-old boy develops palpable purpura on both legs one week after strep pharyngitis. Biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis; tissue is IgA-positive, serum MPO-ANCA is negative.
Mechanism: immune complex vasculitis (IgA vasculitis / Henoch-Schönlein purpura) — IgA complexes form in response to the preceding infection, deposit in small vessels, and activate complement, recruiting neutrophils that damage the vessel wall.

Patient 2: a 56-year-old woman presents with hematuria and hemoptysis; kidney biopsy shows pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis; serum is MPO-ANCA positive, tissue IgA negative.
Mechanism: ANCA-associated vasculitis — autoantibodies against MPO bind primed neutrophils directly on the small vessel wall and activate them, with no antibody/immune-complex deposition (hence “pauci-immune”).

5.4 Giant cell arteritis vs. Takayasu arteritis

Giant Cell (Temporal) ArteritisTakayasu Arteritis
Age> 50 years< 50 years
Demographics—Primarily women of Asian ancestry
VesselMost notably the temporal artery (can involve other large vessels)Primarily the aorta and its major branches
DistributionPatchy — a negative temporal biopsy does not exclude disease—
Clinical clueJaw claudication, vision lossWeak upper extremity pulse (“pulseless disease”)
Shared: both affect large vessels, are granulomatous, and can show giant cells; inflammation is transmural in both.

5.5 Key histologic features of vasculitis

5.6 Buerger's disease (thromboangiitis obliterans)

A medium-vessel, non-granulomatous vasculitis (microabscesses only) strongly linked to heavy smoking in young males. Presents with distal extremity ischemia progressing to gangrene.

5.7 EGPA histology

5.8 Raynaud's phenomenon

A vasospastic disorder producing a characteristic white → blue → red color sequence in the fingers/toes:

ColorMechanism
WhiteVasospasm sharply reduces blood flow → pallor, ischemia
BlueCyanosis from prolonged deoxygenation of stagnant blood
RedReperfusion once the vasospasm resolves
Practice Questions — Section 5

1. A 68-year-old woman presents with jaw claudication and a tender, cord-like temporal artery. A temporal artery biopsy is negative for vasculitis. What is the best next step in reasoning about this result?

Giant cell arteritis has a patchy (“skip lesion”) distribution, so a single negative temporal artery biopsy does not rule it out — clinical suspicion should still guide management or repeat biopsy.

2. Which vasculitis is classically associated with asthma and a peripheral/tissue eosinophilia?

EGPA (formerly Churg-Strauss syndrome) is the small-vessel, granulomatous, MPO-ANCA-associated vasculitis classically linked to asthma and marked eosinophilia.

3. A patient's vasculitis workup shows pauci-immune glomerulonephritis with no immune complex deposition on biopsy. Which mechanism of vessel injury does this most strongly support?

“Pauci-immune” means immune-mediated vessel damage without antibody/immune-complex deposition — the hallmark of ANCA-associated vasculitis, in which autoantibodies activate neutrophils directly at the vessel wall.

6. Vascular Neoplasms & Vascular Ectasias

6.1 Benign vascular tumors

TumorKey Features
Capillary hemangiomaMany small vascular channels; can spontaneously regress
Juvenile ("strawberry") hemangiomaA capillary hemangioma subtype in newborns; raised, red, bumpy lesion
Cavernous hemangiomaLarger, dilated vascular channels; does not regress
Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma)Red nodule on oral mucosa/gingiva; frequently ulcerates or bleeds

Bacillary angiomatosisInfectious (not truly neoplastic) proliferation from Bartonella; occurs in immunocompromised/HIV patients; can mimic Kaposi sarcoma clinically

TypeFeatures
Capillary/simple lymphangiomaSmaller lymphatic channels
Cavernous lymphangiomaLarger lymphatic channels
Cystic hygromaVery large lesion in young children/infants; associated with Turner syndrome

6.3 Vascular ectasia (not a neoplasm)

Vascular ectasia is localized vessel dilation — a malformation, not a tumor.

EntityFeatures
Nevus flammeusFlat, light pink-to-purple birthmark of the head/neck (“port-wine stain”)
  — Sturge-Weber syndromeExtensive port-wine staining with brain ischemia, gray-matter atrophy, and glaucoma
Osler-Weber-Rendu diseaseHereditary; numerous permanent telangiectasias across skin and oral mucosa; recurrent bleeding
Spider telangiectasiaHyperestrogenic states; face/neck/upper chest; central core with radiating branches

6.4 Borderline & malignant vascular neoplasms

TumorBehaviorKey Facts
HemangioendotheliomaBorderlineIntermediate behavior between benign and malignant
Kaposi sarcomaBorderline/malignantHHV-8 associated; classic in AIDS/immunocompromised patients; slit-like vascular spaces with spindle cells on histology
AngiosarcomaMalignantRisk factors: chronic lymphedema, radiation, arsenic, vinyl chloride; hepatic angiosarcoma classically linked to these exposures
HemangiopericytomaMalignant (variable grade)Cells sit outside the endothelium; CD31 negative (distinguishes from angiosarcoma)
Corrected in session The angiosarcoma carcinogen is vinyl chloride itself, not the polymer polyvinyl chloride (PVC). PVC manufacturing exposes workers to vinyl chloride monomer, which is the actual carcinogen — the finished PVC plastic (e.g., pipe) is not. Robbins lists “polyvinyl chloride” as the risk factor, but this distinction is worth knowing precisely.

6.5 Why does AIDS increase risk of these lesions?

AIDS causes profound, lasting immunosuppression, increasing susceptibility to opportunistic infection and its complications:

  • Bacillary angiomatosis — an opportunistic infection from Bartonella henselae (cat-scratch disease) or Bartonella quintana (trench fever)
  • Kaposi sarcoma — a borderline neoplasm driven by HHV-8, which immunocompromised patients are more likely to acquire and less able to control
Case — three oral vascular lesions Three patients present with oral mucosal lesions; biopsies are taken and stained with H&E, CD31, and HHV-8.

CD31 (a pan-endothelial marker) shows staining limited to the vascular lining in the more organized/benign lesion, vs. diffuse expression across sheets of atypical cells in the poorly differentiated lesion — diffuse CD31 positivity reflects a less-differentiated, more aggressive vascular tumor.

HHV-8 was positive only in Patient C — confirming Kaposi sarcoma. Patients A and B were HHV-8 negative.

Putting it together (least → most malignant):

  1. Patient B — pyogenic granuloma (benign): organized small vessels, prominent inflammation, HHV-8 negative
  2. Patient C — Kaposi sarcoma (borderline/malignant): slit-like vasculature, hemosiderin, HHV-8 positive
  3. Patient A — angiosarcoma (malignant): disorganized, hemorrhagic, poorly formed vasculature — the most aggressive morphology of the three

Additional information that would refine prognosis for all three: assessment of metastatic spread — organ involvement portends a poorer prognosis.

6.6 Kaposi sarcoma at a glance

Practice Questions — Section 6

1. A birthmark biopsy from a young infant shows large, dilated vascular channels containing no red blood cells. This is most consistent with:

Lymphangiomas contain lymphatic (not blood) channels, so they characteristically lack red blood cells within the dilated spaces — the key distinguishing feature from hemangioma.

2. A worker with long-term occupational exposure to vinyl chloride monomer during PVC pipe manufacturing develops a liver mass. Which tumor is most strongly associated with this specific exposure?

Hepatic angiosarcoma is classically associated with vinyl chloride monomer exposure (along with arsenic, Thorotrast, and chronic lymphedema) — the monomer itself, not the finished PVC polymer, is the carcinogen.

3. A vascular tumor stains diffusely positive for CD31 across sheets of atypical spindle cells, with no HHV-8 positivity, and cells sitting outside a clear endothelial lining are absent. This staining pattern is most consistent with:

Diffuse (rather than lining-restricted) CD31 positivity reflects a poorly differentiated, aggressive vascular tumor — angiosarcoma — while the absence of HHV-8 argues against Kaposi sarcoma. Hemangiopericytoma is classically CD31-negative, which further excludes it here.
